title: Lesson 6: Giving Feedback Without Embarrassing Others
summary: Feedback should improve behaviour, not make someone feel small. Correct the issue firmly, privately when practical, and without humiliation.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Respectful correction, constructive feedback, emotional intelligence, protecting dignity and improving team performance

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a therapist at Zura Spa forgets to replenish the massage oil after completing a session.
Another therapist discovers the problem while preparing for her next client.

In front of the receptionist and two other employees, she announces: "Everybody, come and see! This is what I'm always talking about. Some people don't know how to do their jobs. How many times must we keep correcting this?"

The therapist who made the mistake feels embarrassed. She becomes defensive, raises her voice and begins arguing. Other employees become uncomfortable, and what could have been a simple correction turns into a workplace conflict.

Now consider a different approach. The colleague approaches the therapist privately and says: "I noticed the massage oil wasn't replenished after the last session. It delayed my preparation a little. Please, can we make sure the supplies are checked before handing over the room?"
The therapist responds: "I'm sorry. I forgot to check it. I'll make sure I do that next time."
The issue is addressed without unnecessary embarrassment.
Both situations involved the same mistake. However, the method of correction produced very different outcomes.
The purpose of feedback should be to improve behaviour or performance, not to make someone feel small.
At Zura Spa, every employee should learn how to raise concerns, correct mistakes and communicate expectations without insulting, humiliating or unnecessarily embarrassing others.
This responsibility applies to supervisors, receptionists, therapists and every other member of the team.

sections.title: 2. What is constructive feedback?
paragraphs: Constructive feedback is information given to help someone understand what they are doing well, what needs improvement and how they can improve.
It should be specific, respectful, factual and useful.
Correction focuses on an issue that needs to change. Humiliation focuses on making someone feel inferior.
A person can be corrected firmly without being insulted.

sections.title: Examples

items.label: Constructive feedback
items.body: "The treatment room was not fully prepared before the appointment. Please ensure the towels and supplies are checked before the next client arrives."

items.label: Destructive feedback
items.body: "You are so careless. You never do anything properly."

paragraphs: The first statement addresses a particular issue and explains what needs to improve. The second attacks the employee's character.

sections.title: 1. It protects people's dignity
paragraphs: Employees deserve to be treated respectfully, even when they make mistakes.

sections.title: 2. It strengthens workplace relationships
paragraphs: Respectful feedback helps colleagues cooperate without unnecessary resentment.

sections.title: 3. It improves communication
paragraphs: Employees are more likely to listen when feedback is clear and not insulting.

sections.title: 4. It encourages improvement
paragraphs: Employees can concentrate on correcting mistakes rather than defending themselves against personal attacks.

sections.title: 5. It builds trust
paragraphs: Employees become more comfortable raising genuine concerns when they know those concerns will be handled fairly.

sections.title: 6. It supports excellent client service
paragraphs: Clear feedback helps employees maintain consistent standards in room preparation, appointments, hygiene and client care.

sections.title: 4. The difference between correction and embarrassment
paragraphs: The respectful approach addresses the issue without turning the employee into a public example of failure.

sections.title: Example — a missed appointment change
paragraphs: A receptionist forgets to inform a therapist about an appointment change.
Embarrassing approach: "Everyone should know that this receptionist is the reason we're having problems today!"
Respectful approach: "The appointment change wasn't communicated to the therapist. Can we review what happened and ensure future changes are passed on promptly?"

sections.title: 5. Correct the behaviour, not the person's identity
paragraphs: One of the most important principles of constructive feedback is separating a person's behaviour from their identity.
Describe what happened, explain why it matters and identify what needs to change.

sections.title: Avoid statements such as
list: "You are lazy."
"You are useless."
"You are irresponsible."
"You are always confused."
"You don't have common sense."
"You can never do anything right."
paragraphs: These statements attack the individual rather than explaining the problem.

sections.title: Better alternatives
table: "The assigned cleaning task was not completed before the next appointment."
"The equipment issue was not reported when it was discovered."
"The instruction was not followed as discussed. Can we clarify what happened?"
"You arrived after your scheduled start time on three occasions this week."
"This part of the room-preparation process needs improvement."

sections.title: 6. Correct privately when practical
paragraphs: Employees may feel embarrassed when their mistakes are discussed unnecessarily in front of colleagues.
For most individual performance concerns, a private conversation is more appropriate.
Urgency may require immediate intervention. It does not justify insults or humiliation.

sections.title: Example — an incomplete room checklist
paragraphs: A supervisor notices that a therapist has repeatedly failed to complete a room-preparation task.
Rather than announcing the mistake during a general staff meeting, the supervisor can arrange a brief private discussion.
"I've noticed that the room checklist was incomplete after two recent sessions. Is there anything making it difficult to complete? Let's discuss how to ensure it's done consistently."

sections.title: Why privacy matters
list: Reduce unnecessary embarrassment.
Encourage honest explanations.
Prevent colleagues from taking sides.
Protect the employee's dignity.
Make it easier to agree on practical improvements.

sections.title: When immediate correction may be necessary
paragraphs: Not every issue can wait for a private discussion.
For example, if a client is at risk because of an unsafe practice, the employee should be stopped or redirected immediately.
However, the correction should still be proportionate and respectful.

sections.title: 7. Choose the right time for feedback
paragraphs: Timing can affect how feedback is received.
Poor timing: A supervisor begins a lengthy discussion about an employee's performance while the employee is attending to a client. This may distract the employee and affect service delivery.
Better timing: The supervisor addresses any urgent concern immediately, then arranges a suitable moment to discuss the details.
Feedback should be timely enough to remain useful and considerate enough to be understood.
list: Address urgent safety concerns immediately.
Raise routine concerns reasonably promptly.
Avoid unnecessary confrontation in front of clients.
Do not deliberately delay important feedback until frustration builds.
Allow sufficient time for clarification.
Avoid discussing sensitive individual performance matters in a crowded environment.

sections.title: 8. Manage your emotions before correcting someone
paragraphs: Employees should avoid giving feedback while overwhelmed by anger.
When someone is angry, even a valid concern may be communicated disrespectfully.
If your main intention is to embarrass or punish someone emotionally, you are not ready to give constructive feedback.

sections.title: Example — an untidy treatment room
paragraphs: A therapist discovers that a colleague has left a treatment room untidy. She feels frustrated because her next appointment is approaching.
Emotional reaction: "I'm tired of your nonsense! You always leave everything for other people!"
Professional response: "The room wasn't ready when I arrived, and I have a client shortly. Please help address the preparation issue now. We can discuss the handover afterward."
The professional response identifies the immediate problem without insulting the colleague.

sections.title: Questions to ask yourself before giving feedback
list: Am I trying to solve a problem or express my anger?
Do I understand what actually happened?
Is this the right time and place?
Can I explain the concern without insulting the person?
What improvement am I requesting?

sections.title: 9. The CARE method for giving feedback

items.label: C — Choose the right setting
items.body: Consider whether the feedback should be given privately, immediately or through a supervisor.

items.label: A — Address the specific issue
items.body: Describe the observable behaviour or outcome without personal attacks.

items.label: R — Respect the person's perspective
items.body: Allow the employee to explain relevant circumstances and ask questions.

items.label: E — Explain the expected improvement
items.body: Agree on a clear, practical next step and follow up when necessary.

sections.title: CARE example
paragraphs: A receptionist has failed to inform a therapist about a change in appointment time.

The supervisor chooses a suitable private moment and says: "The appointment was moved from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m., but the therapist wasn't informed. This affected her preparation. Can you explain how the change was handled?"
After listening, the supervisor adds: "Going forward, please ensure appointment changes are communicated to the assigned therapist as soon as they're confirmed."
This is clear, respectful and solution-focused.

sections.title: 10. Give specific feedback instead of vague criticism
paragraphs: Vague criticism leaves employees uncertain about what needs to improve.
Good feedback should answer three questions: What happened? Why does it matter? What should happen differently?

items.label: Specific
items.body: "During yesterday's discussion, you interrupted your colleague several times before she finished speaking. Please allow others to complete their explanations before responding."

items.label: Specific
items.body: "You arrived 20 minutes after your scheduled start time today, and the opening preparation was delayed. Please ensure you are ready to begin work at your scheduled time."

sections.title: 11. Avoid correcting people through sarcasm or mockery
paragraphs: Sarcasm may sound humorous to the person speaking but humiliating to the person receiving it.
These statements do not clearly explain the expected improvement. Instead, they may encourage resentment or unnecessary arguments.
Humour should not be used to disguise insults.
Better approach: "The task wasn't completed before the appointment. Please ensure it is finished on time going forward."
list: "Oh, so you've finally decided to work today?"
"Congratulations! You've made another mistake."
"Should we clap for you because you remembered the towels?"
"Maybe we should send you back to school."

sections.title: 12. Avoid public criticism in staff WhatsApp groups
paragraphs: Staff WhatsApp groups may be useful for sharing schedules, updates, reminders and operational information.
However, they should not become platforms for humiliating individual employees.
A group reminder may be appropriate when the message concerns everyone.
An individual correction should not automatically become a public announcement.
Serious incidents may require formal reporting or documentation through authorised channels, even when confidentiality must be maintained.
The purpose of a staff group is to support coordination, not to create a public record of someone's embarrassment.

sections.title: WhatsApp examples

items.label: Inappropriate message
items.body: "Everyone should see how careless some people are. This is the third time this particular therapist has failed to prepare her room!"

items.label: Better approach — general reminder
items.body: "Good afternoon, team. Please ensure all treatment rooms are properly prepared and supplies replenished before the next appointment. Report any shortages promptly. Thank you."

paragraphs: If an individual employee needs correction, the relevant supervisor can address it directly through an appropriate private channel.

sections.title: 13. Give feedback based on facts, not assumptions
paragraphs: Sometimes employees correct others without knowing the full situation.
Fair feedback begins with an accurate understanding of the situation.

sections.title: Example — an untidy room with incomplete information
paragraphs: A therapist sees an untidy room and assumes the previous therapist failed to clean it. She confronts her colleague. Later, she discovers that another employee used the room afterward. The accusation was based on incomplete information.
Better response: "I noticed the room wasn't ready when I arrived. Do you know what happened after the last session?"
This creates an opportunity to establish the facts.

sections.title: Practical principles
list: Confirm what you personally observed.
Distinguish facts from assumptions.
Ask questions when information is incomplete.
Avoid spreading accusations.
Allow the employee to explain.
Correct inaccurate information when it becomes clear.

sections.title: 14. Giving feedback to colleagues at the same level
paragraphs: Employees should be able to raise legitimate work-related concerns with colleagues respectfully.
However, they should avoid behaving as though they have disciplinary authority over one another.
A colleague can raise a concern. A supervisor or management representative may have responsibility for formal performance correction or disciplinary decisions.
Employees should respect these boundaries.

sections.title: Example — unreplenished supplies
paragraphs: A therapist notices that another therapist has not replenished the supplies.
Disrespectful approach: "You better start doing your job properly. I'm not your servant!"
Respectful approach: "The supplies weren't replenished after the previous session. Please, can we make sure they're checked before the room is handed over?"
If the problem continues, the employee may report the concern to the appropriate supervisor.

sections.title: 15. Giving feedback as a supervisor or team leader
paragraphs: Supervisors have additional responsibility because their words can influence employees' confidence, motivation and willingness to communicate.
You can hold employees accountable without making them afraid to tell the truth.
list: Correct behaviour without attacking character.
Explain expectations clearly.
Listen before reaching conclusions.
Consider workload and available resources.
Recognise improvements.
Avoid favouritism.
Maintain confidentiality where appropriate.
Apply standards fairly.
Demonstrate the behaviour they expect from others.

sections.title: Example — repeated booking errors
paragraphs: A receptionist repeatedly fails to confirm booking details.
Unhelpful supervisory approach: "You're obviously not intelligent enough for this work."

Constructive supervisory approach: "We've had three booking errors this week. Let's review how appointments are being recorded and identify where the mistakes are occurring. I expect each booking to be verified before confirmation."
The second approach is firm and clear without being degrading.

sections.title: 16. Giving feedback to someone who becomes defensive
paragraphs: Even respectfully delivered feedback may be received defensively.
The person giving feedback should avoid escalating the conversation.
A calm response does not require ignoring serious misconduct or unsafe behaviour. Those concerns should be addressed through the appropriate procedures.

sections.title: Example — "Why are you always picking on me?"
paragraphs: A supervisor raises a concern about an incomplete room checklist. The employee responds: "Why are you always picking on me?"

Constructive response: "I'm not questioning your worth or everything you do. I'm addressing the incomplete checklist because it affects room readiness. I want to understand what happened and how we can prevent it."
If the conversation becomes heated: "I can see this is upsetting. We can take a brief pause and continue when we're both ready to discuss it respectfully."

sections.title: What to avoid
list: Responding with insults.
Raising your voice to overpower the employee.
Making threats out of anger.
Bringing up unrelated past issues.
Continuing an unproductive public argument.

sections.title: 17. Balancing correction with appreciation
paragraphs: A healthy feedback culture should not focus only on mistakes.
Employees also need to understand what they are doing well.
The appreciation should be genuine, not a technique for disguising criticism.
A workplace where employees hear only criticism may struggle to build confidence and motivation.
list: Recognise good work when it occurs.
Be specific about what was done well.
Address areas for improvement clearly.
Avoid exaggerated praise.
Do not compare employees unnecessarily.
Recognise progress, not only perfect results.

sections.title: Example — client care and a delayed checklist
paragraphs: A therapist consistently provides excellent client care but occasionally delays completing the room checklist.

A supervisor might say: "Your attention to client comfort has been good, and I appreciate that. I also need you to complete the room checklist promptly after each session so the next appointment can begin smoothly."

sections.title: Case study A: Public embarrassment
paragraphs: A supervisor notices that a receptionist has made a booking error.
During a staff meeting, the supervisor announces: "This is why some people shouldn't be trusted with important responsibilities." The receptionist becomes visibly upset.
Expected lesson: A legitimate correction does not justify public humiliation.
list: Was the booking error a legitimate concern?
What was inappropriate about the supervisor's response?
How could the correction have been handled privately?
What should the receptionist do to address the original error?
How could management restore a respectful working relationship?

sections.title: Case study B: The angry therapist
paragraphs: A therapist discovers that her colleague left a treatment room untidy. She confronts her in front of a client.
Expected lesson: Employees should protect client service and address individual concerns at an appropriate time and place.
list: Why was the timing inappropriate?
How could the confrontation affect the client's experience?
What immediate action should be taken?
How should the colleagues discuss the issue afterward?

sections.title: Case study C: The WhatsApp message
paragraphs: A staff member posts a colleague's mistake in the general WhatsApp group and adds laughing emojis. Other employees begin commenting.
Expected lesson: Workplace communication channels should not be used for mockery or public embarrassment.
list: What makes this communication inappropriate?
How might it affect the employee involved?
How should the original issue have been reported?
What should a supervisor do after discovering the message?

sections.title: Case study D: The unfair accusation
paragraphs: A supervisor criticises a therapist for failing to prepare a room.
The therapist explains that the room was used again after she completed her assigned preparation. The supervisor realises the original information was incomplete.
Expected lesson: Giving feedback responsibly includes being willing to revise your judgment and apologise when you were wrong.
list: What should the supervisor do after discovering the error?
Why is it important to correct an inaccurate accusation?
How can the supervisor acknowledge the mistake respectfully?
What process could help prevent similar misunderstandings?

sections.title: 19. Practical group activity: Correct without humiliating
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise giving clear, respectful feedback that protects dignity and encourages improvement.
Divide participants into pairs. One person gives feedback, while the other receives it and asks clarifying questions.
Each pair should rewrite and practise the following statements.
Expected outcome: Participants should be able to give feedback firmly, clearly and respectfully without unnecessary embarrassment.
table: "The booking details were entered incorrectly. Please verify them before confirmation."
"This part of the preparation needs improvement. Let's review the expected procedure."
"Let's discuss what happened privately and identify the next step."
"The assigned task wasn't completed by the agreed time. What prevented it?"
"The instruction wasn't followed as discussed. Could we clarify it?"
"This repeated issue is affecting the team. We need to agree on a practical improvement plan."

sections.title: Role-play
list: Identify a realistic workplace mistake.
Choose an appropriate setting.
Describe the specific issue.
Explain its impact.
Allow the employee to respond.
Agree on the expected improvement.

sections.title: 20. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 6 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the main purpose of constructive feedback? To embarrass someone so they never repeat a mistake / To help someone understand an issue and improve / To demonstrate who has more authority

When should individual performance feedback usually be given? Privately when practical, while addressing urgent safety issues immediately / In front of as many colleagues as possible / Only through public WhatsApp messages
Which statement focuses on behaviour rather than identity? You are lazy. / You never do anything right. / The room checklist was incomplete before the next appointment.
What does the CARE method stand for? Criticise, Accuse, React, Embarrass / Choose the setting, Address the issue, Respect the perspective, Explain improvement / Complain, Argue, Repeat, Escalate

What should a supervisor do after discovering that a correction was based on inaccurate information? Acknowledge the error, correct the information and apologise where appropriate / Continue blaming the employee to preserve authority / Ignore the new facts

sections.title: 21. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what constructive feedback means.
Identify five ways feedback can become embarrassing or humiliating.
Explain why employees should generally be corrected privately when practical.
Describe the difference between correcting someone's behaviour and attacking their identity.
Explain the CARE method in your own words.
Describe how you would correct a colleague who repeatedly forgets to replenish room supplies.
Explain how a supervisor should respond when an employee becomes defensive during correction.
Describe why sarcasm and mockery are inappropriate methods of workplace correction.
Explain how staff WhatsApp groups should be used when communicating operational reminders.
Describe what you should do if you discover that your feedback was based on incorrect information.
Identify three habits you intend to develop when giving feedback to colleagues.

sections.title: 22. Seven-day respectful feedback challenge
table: Notice how you speak when correcting others
Avoid sarcasm, mockery and personal attacks
Choose an appropriate time and setting for a correction
Reflect on whether your feedback has been respectful, clear and useful

sections.title: 23. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Every employee will sometimes need to correct another person's work or raise a concern.
However, the way feedback is delivered matters.
At Zura Spa, employees should never use correction as an opportunity to insult, mock, intimidate or unnecessarily embarrass others.
Feedback should focus on the specific issue, the effect on work or service and the improvement required.
Supervisors must lead by example, while colleagues should communicate concerns respectfully and follow appropriate reporting channels.
Next topic: Distinguishing Constructive Correction from Personal Attack.

remember: Correction should help people become better, not make them feel worthless. You do not need to embarrass someone to communicate that a mistake was made. At Zura Spa, we value feedback that is honest, respectful and useful. Speak to people in a way that preserves their dignity, makes expectations clear and encourages genuine improvement. The goal is not to win an argument or prove superiority, but to build a stronger team that delivers excellent service together.
